text: Hands that look clean feel clean, and soap is not always nearby. A quick rinse feels like enough on a busy day.
Wash with soap for as long as it takes to hum "Happy Birthday" twice, especially before eating and after coughing.
CDC: About Handwashing (2024); CONTENT_GUIDE safe facts: soap and water for at least 20 seconds
You can get HIV from sharing food, hugging or mosquito bites.
HIV does not spread through hugs, kisses, shared food or utensils, toilets or mosquito bites.
HIV was once surrounded by fear and little information, and some of those old warnings are still repeated. Wanting to stay safe is natural.
Ask a health worker or a DOH HIV treatment hub how HIV does and does not spread.
WHO fact sheet: HIV and AIDS (2026); CDC: Ways HIV is not transmitted (2024)
HIV is a death sentence.
With treatment, people living with HIV can live long, healthy lives. Treatment is free at DOH treatment hubs.
Many of us remember stories from years ago, before good treatment was easy to get. Those sad memories stay strong.
Ask a DOH treatment hub or social hygiene clinic about free HIV care and support.
WHO fact sheet: HIV and AIDS (2026): a manageable chronic condition with treatment; RA 11166 (2018): free treatment at hubs
People living with HIV will always pass it to their partners.
People with HIV who take treatment and keep an undetectable viral load do not pass HIV on through sex.
This good news is newer than the old fears, and few people talk about it. Most of us learned about HIV when it was scarier.
Ask a health worker at a DOH treatment hub what "undetectable" means and how it is checked.
WHO policy brief: The role of HIV viral suppression in improving individual health and reducing transmission (2023)
An HIV test costs a lot, and everyone will find out the result.
HIV testing is free at government treatment hubs and many clinics, and the law keeps results confidential.
Worry about money and about what others will say is real. Fear of gossip keeps many people from getting tested.
Visit or call a social hygiene clinic or DOH treatment hub. Ask how testing works and how your privacy is kept.
Philippine HIV and AIDS Policy Act (RA 11166, 2018): voluntary, confidential testing; DOH: free testing at government hubs
Only some kinds of people get HIV.
HIV can affect anyone. Testing and prevention are for everyone, without judgment.
News stories often focus on a few groups, so HIV can feel like a problem for other people. That makes it easy to skip testing.
If you think you may have been at risk, ask a health worker about a free, confidential test.
WHO fact sheet: HIV and AIDS (2026); UNAIDS Global AIDS Update (2025)
There is no medicine that can help prevent HIV.
PrEP is a medicine that greatly lowers the chance of getting HIV. A health worker can tell if it suits you.
Most of us only heard about condoms and testing, so a prevention medicine sounds too good to be true. New health news travels slowly.
Ask a DOH treatment hub or social hygiene clinic whether PrEP is available near you.
WHO fact sheet: HIV and AIDS (2026): WHO-recommended pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) options
You can tell if someone has HIV just by looking at them.
Many people with HIV look and feel well for years. Only a test can tell anyone's HIV status.
Old pictures in the news showed very sick people, so that image stuck. It is natural to trust what we see.
Do not guess about anyone. If you want to know your own status, ask for a free, confidential test.
WHO fact sheet: HIV and AIDS (2026): many people do not know their status; testing is the only way to know
A map of online HIV talk shows where HIV cases are.
It shows where people post about HIV, not where cases are. Official case counts come from DOH.
Colourful maps look scientific and exact. It is easy to forget they only count posts, and some places post more than others.
Read the map's title and notes to see what was counted. For case numbers, look at DOH HIV reports.
DOH Epidemiology Bureau: HIV/AIDS and ART Registry of the Philippines (HARP); AdvocAid PH note: discourse maps are not prevalence
AI in a hospital makes decisions on its own.
Health workers stay responsible. AI gives suggestions that trained people check before they decide.
Movies and news make AI sound like a robot doctor. When a machine seems smart, it is easy to picture it in charge.
Ask your doctor or nurse who checks the AI's suggestion and who is responsible for your care.
WHO: Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health (2021): human autonomy, responsibility and accountability
AI cannot be biased because it is a machine.
AI learns from data made by people. If the data leaves groups out, the AI can be unfair to them.
Machines feel neutral because they have no feelings. Numbers and computers can seem fairer than people.
Ask whether the tool was tested on people like you, including older adults, women and people in the provinces.
WHO: Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health (2021): inclusiveness and equity
An AI health app with five-star ratings must be accurate.
Ratings show if people like an app, not if its health advice is right. Ask if it was tested.
Stars and happy reviews are quick to read and feel like advice from friends. Checking studies takes time we do not have.
Look for who made the app and whether it is approved for health use. Ask your health worker before relying on it.
WHO: Regulatory considerations on artificial intelligence for health (2023): evidence and validation before use
You cannot ask how an AI reached its result.
You can ask. Health workers should explain in plain words what the AI looked at and how they used it.
AI can seem like a black box that even experts do not understand. It may feel rude to question a doctor or a machine.
Ask: "What did the AI look at, and do you agree with it?" A good health worker will explain.
WHO: Ethics and governance of AI for health (2021): transparency, explainability and intelligibility; RA 10173 right to be informed
With a health chatbot, I can skip my regular check-ups.
A chatbot cannot examine you or run tests. Keep your check-ups and use chatbots only for general information.
Chatbots are free, fast and awake at midnight, while clinics mean travel, lines and costs. Saving time and money matters.
Keep your health center appointments. Bring your chatbot questions to your health worker.
WHO: Ethics and governance of AI for health: Guidance on large multi-modal models (2024)
Health data I give an app is never shared with anyone.
Some apps share data with other companies. The privacy notice must tell you, and the law gives you rights.
Apps look friendly and official, and privacy notices are long. Most of us tap "agree" to get on with our day.
Read the sharing part of the privacy notice before signing up. You can ask the app what it keeps and to delete it.
Data Privacy Act of 2012 (RA 10173): rights to be informed, to access and to erasure; NPC Advisory No. 2024-04 (2024)
An AI that is right most of the time will be right for me.
An AI can do well on average but miss people unlike those in its training data. Ask how it was tested.
A score like "90% accurate" sounds like a promise to each of us. Averages are easy to read as personal guarantees.
Ask whether the AI was tested on people like you. Tell your health worker if a result does not fit how you feel.
WHO: Regulatory considerations on artificial intelligence for health (2023): test on the intended population
Trusting AI means trusting it fully.
Good trust fits the task: rely on AI where it is proven, and double-check it when the stakes are high.
It feels simpler to trust a tool all the way or not at all. Partial trust sounds confusing, but it is what careful people do.
Before acting on an AI answer, ask: how serious is this, and who can double-check it?
WHO: Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health (2021); ARAW calibrated trust (docs/SPEC.md section 1)
Aedes mosquitoes spread only dengue.
The same Aedes mosquitoes can also spread chikungunya and Zika. Stopping them protects against all three.
Dengue is the mosquito disease we hear about most. Names like chikungunya and Zika can sound far away.
Ask your barangay health worker which mosquito diseases are in your area and how to stop mosquitoes breeding.
WHO: Global strategic preparedness, readiness and response plan for dengue and other Aedes-borne arboviruses (2024)
A bottle cap of water is too small to breed mosquitoes.
Aedes mosquitoes can breed in very little clean water, like caps, plant trays and old tires.
A tiny bit of water does not look like a danger. We picture mosquitoes coming from big canals and ponds.
Every week, search for small water holders around the house and empty, scrub or cover them. This is DOH's first S.
WHO fact sheet: Dengue and severe dengue (2025); DOH 4S: Search and destroy mosquito breeding places
Reporting a breeding site to the barangay does not help.
Community reports help barangays and LGUs find and clean up breeding sites before cases rise.
It can feel like reports go nowhere, or that one person cannot make a difference. Many of us also do not want to bother anyone.
Report standing water in shared places to your barangay health worker, with the location and a photo if you can.
WHO: Global strategic preparedness, readiness and response plan for dengue and other Aedes-borne arboviruses (2024): community protection
Stopping mosquito diseases is only a job for health workers.
It takes everyone. People, animals and our surroundings share health, so clean yards and drains protect all.
Health feels like something for clinics and doctors. Cleaning drains and yards does not feel like health work.
Join your barangay clean-up. Keep drains clear, and change water for animals and plants often.
WHO fact sheet: One Health (2023); Quadripartite One Health Joint Plan of Action (2022)
